meta.subtitle: Broad-line semiconductor and passive-component maker in a cyclical upturn, spending heavily on capacity as margins and free cash inflect.

analystCommentary: Vishay is a cyclical recovery priced on next year's earnings, not this year's. Revenue reached $888.6 million in the second fiscal quarter, ended July 4, 2026, up from $762.3 million a year earlier. Gross margin rose to 23.3% from 19.5% as volume filled the plants, and a book-to-bill of {+ 1.32 +} with a 6.1-month backlog points to further growth; management guides next-quarter revenue to $945 million to $975 million. Diluted EPS was {+ $0.19 +} against $0.01 a year earlier. The counter-case is real: trailing net margin is just 0.9%, FY25 free cash flow was {- -$89 million -} after $273.3 million of capital expenditure, and the shares trade at 174.4x trailing earnings. Our call rests on the forward path — consensus FY27 EPS of $1.74 puts the stock near 19.0x — and on orders staying ahead of shipments. We rate the shares BUY with a $36 to $46 target, about 19.2% of upside to a probability-weighted fair value, against a bear near $26.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Vishay Intertechnology manufactures a broad, high-volume portfolio of discrete semiconductors and passive electronic components, sold into the automotive, industrial, computing, consumer, telecommunications, military, aerospace, and healthcare markets. The company was incorporated in 1962 and is headquartered in Malvern, Pennsylvania. It manages the business in six product-functional segments — MOSFETs, Diodes, Optoelectronic Components, Resistors, Inductors, and Capacitors — and sells under brand names including Siliconix, Dale, Sprague, and Vitramon. Its end markets are cyclical, and fiscal 2024 showed it: revenue fell {- 13.7% -} that year and operating margin collapsed to 0.2%. Fiscal 2025 began the recovery, with revenue up {+ 4.5% +} to $3.1 billion, though the company still posted a net loss of -$9 million. The business is now in a clearer upturn, and management is spending heavily to expand capacity ahead of demand.

thesis.body: The case is a cyclical inflection backed by order momentum. Book-to-bill was 1.32 in the latest quarter and backlog stood at 6.1 months, both signs that shipments should keep rising. Gross margin has widened as volume absorbs fixed costs, and management guides next-quarter revenue higher again. At $33.14 the stock sits far below its 52-week high of $69.47 and trades at a forward multiple that falls sharply on next year's estimates, so a recovery is only partly discounted. The risk is that the cycle turns before the heavy capital spending pays off: free cash flow has been negative and trailing profitability is thin. We think the order book and the forward earnings path tilt the balance up, but for a company this cyclical the bear case is real.

catalysts: Order momentum is the near-term driver: a book-to-bill above one and a lengthening backlog should convert into rising shipments over coming quarters.
Guidance for the next quarter points to sequential growth, with management targeting revenue of $945 million to $975 million and gross margin around 24.0%.
Margin leverage: as volume fills the recently expanded plants, incremental revenue should carry high drop-through and lift operating margin off cyclical lows.
The July equity offering repaid the revolving credit facility, cutting interest cost and giving the company room to fund its capacity build.
risks: The business is highly cyclical; demand can fall abruptly, and largely fixed costs would then compress gross margin and operating income.
Capacity expansion carries execution risk — new wafer fabs and site build-outs can suffer delays, cost overruns, and low initial yields.
Free cash flow has been negative while capital spending runs high, so the recovery must turn into cash before it rewards shareholders.
Dual-class voting concentrates control with the Zandman family, limiting outside shareholders' influence.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue in Vishay's second fiscal quarter, ended July 4, 2026, was $888.6 million, up from $762.3 million in the same quarter a year earlier and $839.2 million in the prior quarter. The company reports this period as its second fiscal quarter; the data feed in this pack labels it Q3, and we follow the company's own designation. That GAAP figure is stated after a {- $30.0 million -} reduction for tariff refunds passed through to customers; on an adjusted basis revenue was $918.6 million, and the pass-through had no effect on gross profit. Gross margin was {+ 23.3% +}, up from 19.5% a year earlier, as higher volume brought manufacturing efficiencies that offset higher metals and materials costs. Operating margin reached {+ 6.0% +}, and diluted EPS was {+ $0.19 +} against $0.01 a year ago. For the six months, net earnings were $35.3 million, or $0.25 per diluted share, versus a net loss of -$2.1 million a year earlier. The trailing-twelve-month picture is still modest — gross margin 20.9%, operating margin 3.3%, net margin 0.9% — a reminder that the recovery is early. Full-year 2025 tells the trough story: revenue of $3.1 billion grew 4.5%, but the company posted a net loss of -$9 million and a diluted loss of -$0.07 per share, with gross margin of 19.4% down from 21.3% in 2024.
financials.balanceCommentary: Vishay entered 2026 with a stretched but serviceable balance sheet: at the end of fiscal 2025 it held about $0.5 billion of cash and short-term investments against $1.0 billion of total debt, for net debt of $435.9 million and total equity of $2.1 billion. The July 1, 2026 equity offering changed the picture: the company sold 17.25 million shares at $50.00 apiece for net proceeds of $830.25 million and used part of the money to reduce the revolving credit facility balance to zero during the third fiscal quarter. That deleveraging cut interest cost and rebuilt liquidity, though it also diluted existing holders. Trailing interest coverage of 2.8x underlines how thin the cushion was before the raise, and the current ratio was 2.62 at year-end 2025.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is the weak link in the story. In fiscal 2025 operating cash flow was about $0.2 billion, but capital expenditure of $273.3 million pushed free cash flow to {- -$89 million -}, a -2.9% free-cash margin; fiscal 2024 was worse at a -5.0% margin. The heavy spending is deliberate — management plans $400 million to $440 million of capital expenditure in 2026, roughly half of it for a new 12-inch wafer fab in Itzehoe, Germany. There is an early sign of a turn: free cash turned positive in the latest quarter, reversing the prior quarter's outflow, as earnings improved and spending moderated. Until the cycle and the capacity build both mature, free cash flow will stay lumpy, and the company's policy of returning most of its free cash flow to shareholders leaves little once capital spending is covered.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing earnings the stock looks extreme at 174.4x, but that reflects a near-zero denominator rather than a rich price; with the company barely profitable over the last year, the trailing P/E carries little information. The more useful lens is forward. At $33.14 the shares trade at 39.4x next-twelve-month earnings and about 19.0x consensus fiscal 2027 EPS of $1.74, as the estimated recovery — $0.84 in 2026 and $1.74 in 2027 — compresses the multiple quickly. Price-to-sales is 1.5x, and EV/EBITDA is not meaningful on depressed trailing EBITDA. The pack carries no peer multiples, so this is a comparison against the company's own history and the Street rather than a named peer set. The Street's consensus target is $40.00, with a median of $42.00 and a range of $26.00 to $45.00.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: The upcycle broadens and holds: book-to-bill stays above one, revenue pushes past the next-quarter guide, and gross margin moves back toward its 2021 and 2022 highs. The 2027 earnings estimate proves conservative, and the market pays a full-cycle multiple for a diversified components franchise, lifting the shares toward and past the Street's high target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: The recovery proceeds at a measured pace. Revenue grows toward the Street's $4.3 billion estimate for 2027, margins keep widening but not to prior peaks, and the 2027 earnings estimate is broadly met. The shares hold a mid-cycle forward multiple and settle near the consensus target of $40.00.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The cycle rolls over before the capacity investment pays off. Orders soften, book-to-bill falls below one, and fixed costs compress margin just as depreciation from the new fabs rises. Free cash flow stays negative, and with trailing profitability already thin the shares de-rate toward the low end of the Street's range near $26.00.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: The probability-weighted fair value is $39.50, about 19.2% above the current price, with a bear case roughly 21.5% below it — a reward-to-risk near 0.9 to 1. That balance, together with a book-to-bill above one and a forward multiple that falls toward the high teens on 2027 estimates, supports a BUY, but only just: the expected upside sits below the threshold for a stronger rating, and the bear case is deep because the business is genuinely cyclical. We set the target range to bracket the base case and the consensus target.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor data in this pack treats Vishay as a single consolidated business, but the company manages itself in six product-functional segments: MOSFETs, Diodes, Optoelectronic Components, Resistors, Inductors, and Capacitors. The first three are discrete semiconductors and the last three are passive components, and the latest quarter's book-to-bill split — 1.23 for semiconductors and 1.40 for passives — shows passive demand leading. The portfolio spans automotive, industrial, computing, consumer, telecommunications, military, aerospace, and healthcare customers, which cushions any single end market but ties the whole to the broader electronics cycle. The pack does not break out revenue by segment or region, so no product or geographic split is quoted here.

moatFactors.name: Portfolio breadth and scale
moatFactors.body: Vishay makes a very broad portfolio of discrete semiconductors and passive components, spanning eight named end markets. Breadth wins sockets — customers can source many part numbers from one qualified supplier — and diversification smooths demand. But breadth in commodity components does not confer pricing power, which is why margins swing so hard with the cycle.

moatFactors.name: Brands and qualified parts
moatFactors.body: Legacy brands such as Siliconix, Dale, Sprague, and Vitramon carry decades of design-ins, and parts qualified into automotive, military, and aerospace systems are slow to displace. That installed base is a genuine switching cost and supports the military, aerospace, and healthcare business. It is a durability advantage more than a pricing advantage.

moatFactors.name: Manufacturing footprint
moatFactors.body: The company is investing to expand internal capacity — a new 12-inch fab in Germany, an expanded Newport fab, and new sites in Mexico, Taiwan, and Italy. Scale manufacturing across regions supports the supply reliability that large OEM customers value. The same capital intensity, though, weighs on returns and free cash flow until utilization rises.

businessMoat.durability: Vishay's advantages are durable but modest. Its breadth, brands, and qualified-part installed base keep it embedded with customers across many industries, and a sixty-plus-year operating history and diversified end markets argue it will endure the cycle as it has before. What the company lacks is pricing power: these are largely commodity components in a competitive, cyclical industry, and gross margin has swung from 30.3% in 2022 to 19.4% in 2025. The heavy capacity build could widen the moat if it locks in supply relationships and lowers unit costs, or it could simply add fixed costs into the next downturn. We rate the moat narrow — enough to survive, not enough to earn high through-cycle returns.

points: The immediate lever is the cyclical upturn: with orders outrunning shipments, revenue should climb through 2026, and consensus sees the full year reaching about $3.7 billion, up 21%.

Longer term, the capacity added over the past three years positions Vishay to supply more part numbers and win share as customers scale, with the new German 12-inch wafer fab adding internal capacity.
Secular demand from e-mobility, sustainability, and connectivity underpins management's growth plan and should lift content per vehicle and per system over time.
The estimated earnings recovery is the clearest signal — consensus moves from a 2025 net loss to solid profits by 2027 — though it depends on the cycle holding.

management.leadership: Joel Smejkal is Chief Executive Officer, President and a director; David McConnell is Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer; and Roy Shoshani is Executive Vice President, Chief Operating Officer for Semiconductors and Chief Technical Officer. Marc Zandman serves as Executive Chairman of the Board and Chief Business Development Officer. Management frames the current strategy as 'Vishay 3.0,' focused on serving a rising customer count and taking advantage of the upcycle. The team's central bet is the multi-year capacity expansion; execution on the new fabs and sites is the test by which this leadership should be judged.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is dominated by the multi-year capacity build. The company recently raised equity to fund growth and repay debt rather than to return cash. Its Stockholder Return Policy calls for returning at least 70% of free cash flow, net of scheduled debt principal, through dividends and buybacks. The quarterly dividend has been held at $0.10 per share; management repurchased no stock in the latest quarter, expects none in 2026, and FY25 buybacks were only -$12.5 million — a sensible pause while free cash flow is negative and capital needs are high. Shareholders should not expect meaningful cash returns until the capacity spending eases.
management.governance: Governance is shaped by a dual-class structure that concentrates control. Class B shares carry ten votes each to common stock's one, and the Zandman family controls the bulk of the Class B through a family trust. Marc Zandman holds 35.2% of the vote and Ruta Zandman 44.3%, and all directors and executive officers as a group hold 44.3% of the voting power despite owning a small fraction of the economic shares. The board is staggered into three classes, which further insulates it. This is a founder-family-controlled company: outside shareholders have economic exposure but little governance leverage, a structural discount factor to keep in mind.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider and family ownership is high in voting terms and low in economic terms. The Zandman family's Class B trust holds 8,616,834 shares that drive its outsized vote, while directors and officers as a group own about 510,378 common shares directly. Among outside holders, BlackRock owns 13.8% of the common stock (7.0% of the vote), Woodline Partners 8.2% (4.1%), and Dimensional Fund Advisors 6.2% (3.1%). The takeaway matches the governance section: economic ownership is broadly held, but voting control sits with the family.

idiosyncratic: Cyclicality is the dominant risk. Electronic-component demand can fall abruptly when customers cut orders or work down inventory, and because much of Vishay's cost base is fixed, a downturn would compress gross margin and operating income quickly, as the 2024 trough showed.

Execution on capacity is a specific risk. The company is building a 12-inch wafer fab in Germany and expanding several other sites; delays, cost overruns, low initial yields, or a demand air-pocket as capacity comes online could all pressure returns, and depreciation will rise regardless of utilization.

Tariff and trade uncertainty is unresolved. The company received IEEPA tariff refunds this year after the Supreme Court struck those tariffs down, but the administration has signaled other tariff mechanisms, and the ultimate cost and pass-through to customers remain uncertain.

Restructuring is a recurring cost. The company ran a restructuring program in 2024 to optimize its manufacturing footprint and expects further restructuring charges tied to future acquisitions, either of which would weigh on reported earnings.
risks.systemic: Vishay's fortunes track the global electronics cycle and, through it, the broader economy. Demand in automotive, industrial, and computing markets depends on macro conditions the company cannot control, and a recession would hit orders across its end markets at once. It also carries the usual multinational exposures — foreign-currency swings, since much of its manufacturing and sales sit outside the United States, and metals and materials cost inflation, which management cited as a margin headwind this year. These are shared, market-wide risks rather than company-specific ones, but they matter more for a cyclical manufacturer than for most.

body: We rate Vishay BUY with a target range of $36 to $46. The case is a cyclical recovery that the order book, the widening margin, and the estimated 2027 earnings all support: book-to-bill is above one, gross margin is climbing, and the forward multiple falls toward the high teens on next year's estimates. Our probability-weighted fair value is $39.50, and the target range brackets both the base case and the consensus.

The rating is a considered BUY, not a strong one. Trailing profitability is thin, free cash flow has been negative through a heavy capital-spending phase, and the dual-class structure limits outside-shareholder influence. The bear case — a cycle that rolls over before the capacity investment pays off — is genuine and sits about 21.5% below today's price, which is why reward-to-risk is only near 0.9 to 1. Investors who can tolerate cyclicality are paid to wait for the upturn to broaden; those who cannot should watch book-to-bill and free cash flow for confirmation before committing.
